**The Kordofan giraffe in the Democratic Republic of Congo is found only in Garamba National Park** – a UNESCO World Heritage Site that has long been on the UNESCO “List in Danger” because of poaching, armed conflict and habitat loss (though the park has recently been removed from that list). Below is a practical guide to spotting these critically‑endangered giants on your June 2025 visit. | Topic | Key details | |-------|-------------| | **Where** | **Garamba National Park** – Haut‑Uélé Province, north‑eastern DRC, bordering South Sudan. The park covers ~492 000 ha and is part of the larger Garamba‑Complex (park + buffer zones). | | **Why it matters** | The park is the **only remaining wild population of the Kordofan giraffe (Giraffa camelopardalis antiquorum)** in the entire country, with an estimated 75–100 individuals (2024 data).¹ | | **Best time to see them** | **Dry season (December – March)** gives the best wildlife visibility and easier travel conditions, but Kordofan giraffes have been observed throughout the year, including the wet season (April – October). If you travel in June, be prepared for rains but you can still see giraffes, especially in the park’s open savannah sections. | | **Getting there** | 1. **Flight to Kisangani** (international hub) or **Entebbe, Uganda** → **Kisangani** (private charter). 2. **Charter to Nagero airstrip** inside Garamba (managed by African Parks).
3. **Ground transport**: Park officials provide vehicle accompaniment from the airstrip to the great savannah zones. | | **Permits & bookings** | • **Entrance permit** – issued by the **Inde Institut Congolais pour la Conservation de la Nature (ICCN)** in partnership with **African Parks**.
• **Safari booking** – must be made **at least 2 months in advance** through African Parks or a certified tour operator.
• **Visitor centre**: Nagero (park headquarters); day‑tours usually run 9 am – 4 pm. | | **Safety & security** | • The park’s security situation is **more stable than in the past** thanks to a joint anti‑poaching effort between ICCN, African Parks, FARDC and local communities.
• Still a **high‑risk area** for travelers; follow all instructions from park rangers and never venture beyond authorized routes.
• It is advisable to travel with a **local guide** familiar with the terrain and current security conditions. | | **What to expect** | • Giraffe can be seen **spotted in the savannahs and along the Garamba and Dungu rivers**; they are most active during early morning and late afternoon.
• Other megafauna: African forest elephant, common hippopotamus, African buffalo, lion, and numerous bird species. | --- ## Practical itinerary for June 2025 | Day | Activity | |-----|----------| | **Day 1** | Arrive in **Kisangani**, transfer to a charter flight to **Nagero** (in‑park airstrip). | | **Day 2** | **Orientation briefing** with the African Parks ranger team. 10‑hour game drive covering the high‑savannah (great giraffe habitat). | | **Day 3** | **Giraffe‑specialised circuit** (carried out in the **"Giraffe Corridor"** identified by recent aerial surveys). Night walk optional to spot nocturnal species. | | **Day 4** | Wilderness trek to **Kiru Valley** (if open path permits). Alternately visit the **Giraffe Conservation Monitoring Centre** for an interactive learning experience. | | **Day 5** | Return to Nagero; debrief, visitor‑center exploration, and optional **community visit** (Azande villages). | | **Day 6** | Departure via Kisangani → return home. | > **Tip:** Because June lies in the rainy season, check local weather forecasts. The park’s roads become muddy; a **four‑wheel‑drive vehicle** is essential for safe travel between savannah zones. --- ## Conservation context - The **Kordofan giraffe** population in Garamba has **grown from ~46 in 2016 to over 100 in 2024** thanks to intensive anti‑poaching measures, ranger training and aerial monitoring.² - Garamba’s **ecological integrity** is crucial not only for giraffes but also for **forest elephants, hippopotamus, and the region’s rich birdlife**. The park’s status as a UNESCO heritage site underscores its global value. - **National and international NGOs** (e.g., Giraffe Conservation Foundation, African Parks) frequently release **state‑of‑conservation reports** that you may wish to review before you travel; they offer insight into current threats (e.g., gold‑panning activities in the buffer zone, occasional armed conflicts). --- ### Quick reference links (accessed 2026‑11‑14) | Resource | URL | |----------|-----| | Garamba National Park official page (UNESCO) | https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/136/ | | African Parks – Garamba overview | https://africanparks.org/the-parks/garamba/ | | Giraffe Conservation Foundation – Garamba programme | https://giraffeconservation.org/programs/kordofan-giraffe-conservation-in-drc/ | | Conservation statistics (2024) | https://drctourism.com/garamba-national-park-kordofan-giraffe-safari/ | | Latest park report (2024) | https://worldheritageoutlook.iucn.org/node/986 | --- ### Bottom line To see the Kordofan giraffe during your June visit to DRC, **plan a safari in Garamba National Park**. Book through African Parks or an accredited operator, obtain permits, and prepare for the rainy‑season logistics. With the park’s recent conservation successes, you’ll have a genuine chance to encounter the world’s most endangered giraffe subspecies in one of Africa’s most inspiring – and historically threatened – landscapes. Enjoy the adventure, and thank the people who keep Garamba alive!

# Kordofan Giraffe Conservation in DRC
Garamba National Park in DRC is the last haven for the Kordofan giraffe in the country. Despite threats from poaching and rebel activities, GCF, African Parks, and the DRC government have successfully achieved a steady increase in giraffe numbers.

In the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), Garamba National Park is home to the last remaining population of Kordofan giraffe (_Giraffa camelopardalis antiquorum_), a subspecies of the northern giraffe (_Giraffa camelopardalis_). Established in 1938 as one of Africa’s first national parks, Garamba stood out for its uniqueness. However, its reputation has been marred by the activities of rebel insurgents (Lord’s Resistance Army) resulting in the loss of the last northern white rhino.
Over the past few decades, poaching has decimated the park’s wildlife, as rebel groups often resort to selling wildlife products to fund their illegal activities. Recognizing the dire situation, the Giraffe Conservation Foundation has collaborated with African Parks and DRC’s wildlife authority, ICCN, since 2016 to save the last natural giraffe population in the country.
Our collaborative efforts have focused on gaining a deeper understanding of population dynamics, habitat use, and immediate threats. The team of African Parks, with the support of the Giraffe Conservation Foundation, implements conservation monitoring and management activities through regular aerial and vehicle-based surveys to monitor all individually-identified giraffe.
The targeted giraffe conservation efforts have resulted in Kordofan giraffe numbers in the park and surrounding areas gradually increasing to over 100 giraffe. This positive trend underscores the importance of continued support for this crucial giraffe conservation initiative, which is slowly transforming into a remarkable success story.

## Where to See Kordofan Giraffes in DRC — Complete Safari Guide
Garamba National Park in northeast DRC is home to critically endangered Kordofan giraffes, forest elephants, hippos, and lions — one of Africa's oldest and most exclusive national parks, managed by African Parks with zero tourist crowds.
Quick Answer
**Yes, there are giraffes in the DRC.** Garamba National Park hosts Kordofan giraffes (Giraffa camelopardalis antiquorum) — one of the rarest giraffe subspecies. The park is a UNESCO World Heritage Site established in 1938, covering 4,902 km² in northeast DRC's Haut-Uélé Province.

## Kordofan Giraffes — Congo's Rarest Giants
The **Kordofan giraffe** (_Giraffa camelopardalis antiquorum_) is one of the most endangered giraffe subspecies in the world, with fewer than 2,000 individuals remaining in the wild. Garamba National Park in northeast DRC is one of its last strongholds.
Distinguished by their paler coloring and irregular patches that extend further down their legs compared to other subspecies, Kordofan giraffes were once widespread across Central and West Africa. Today, their range has collapsed dramatically.
African Parks, in partnership with ICCN (Congo's wildlife authority), has significantly improved the park's security and infrastructure since 2005, creating conditions for wildlife recovery and limited but growing tourism access.

## How to Visit Garamba National Park
### Getting There
Charter flights to Nagero airstrip (inside the park) from Entebbe (Uganda) or Kisangani. Overland access from Dungu for adventurous travelers. Most visitors fly via Entebbe.

## How to Visit Garamba National Park
### Best Time to Visit
November–March (dry season) for optimal wildlife viewing. May–September is greener but some roads may be impassable. Avoid April and October (peak rains).

## How to Visit Garamba National Park
### Where to Stay
Nagero Rest House (managed by African Parks) is the primary accommodation. Tented camping options available. Remote lodge development is part of ongoing investment plans.

## How to Visit Garamba National Park
### Permits & Access
Entry permits issued by African Parks / ICCN. All visits require advance booking. Armed ranger escort included in all safari activities for visitor safety.

In the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), Garamba National Park is home to the last remaining population of Kordofan giraffe (_Giraffa camelopardalis antiquorum_), a subspecies of the northern giraffe (_Giraffa camelopardalis_). Established in 1938 as one of Africa’s first national parks, Garamba stood out for its uniqueness. However, its reputation has been marred by the activities of rebel insurgents (Lord’s Resistance Army) resulting in the loss of the last northern white rhino.
Over the past few decades, poaching has decimated the park’s wildlife, as rebel groups often resort to selling wildlife products to fund their illegal activities. Recognizing the dire situation, the Giraffe Conservation Foundation has collaborated with African Parks and DRC’s wildlife authority, ICCN, since 2016 to save the last natural giraffe population in the country.
Our collaborative efforts have focused on gaining a deeper understanding of population dynamics, habitat use, and immediate threats. The team of African Parks, with the support of the Giraffe Conservation Foundation, implements conservation monitoring and management activities through regular aerial and vehicle-based surveys to monitor all individually-identified giraffe.
The targeted giraffe conservation efforts have resulted in Kordofan giraffe numbers in the park and surrounding areas gradually increasing to over 100 giraffe. This positive trend underscores the importance of continued support for this crucial giraffe conservation initiative, which is slowly transforming into a remarkable success story.

The **Kordofan giraffe** (_Giraffa camelopardalis antiquorum_) is one of the most endangered giraffe subspecies in the world, with fewer than 2,000 individuals remaining in the wild. Garamba National Park in northeast DRC is one of its last strongholds.

# Garamba National Park
###### Garamba National Park
The property, located in the north-eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo, forms part of one of the last extensive and continuous forest–savanna mosaic landscapes in Central Africa. Representing a major ecological transition zone between the Guineo-Congolian forest biome and the Sudanian savanna, it encompasses a diverse range of habitats, including grasslands, wooded savannas, semi-deciduous forests, rivers, gallery forests, marshes, and papyrus wetlands. The World Heritage Committee,
1.   Having examined Documents WHC/26/48.COM/8B and WHC/26/48.COM/INF.8B2,  
2.   Approves the renomination of **Garamba National Park, Democratic Republic of the Congo**, on the World Heritage List on the basis of **criteria****(ix)** and **(x)**;  
3.   Adopts the following Statement of Outstanding Universal Value:
**Brief synthesis**
Garamba National Park is situated in the north-eastern region of the Democratic Republic of the Congo, within Haut-Uélé Province, adjacent to the international boundary with South Sudan. The property forms the ecological core of the larger Garamba Complex, which encompasses approximately 1,470,000 hectares and includes the Azande, Gangala-na-Bodio, and Mondo-Missa hunting domains. Together, these contiguous protected areas constitute one of the last extensive and continuous forest–savanna mosaic landscapes in Central Africa, representing a critical ecological transition zone between the Guineo-Congolian forest biome and the Sudanian savanna. The property covers an area of 512,736 hectares. It is surrounded by a formally designated buffer zone comprising portions of the three adjacent hunting domains, extending up to 20 km from the park boundaries and covering an additional 544,943 hectares. The property is important for the conservation of a range of forest and savanna species, including forest elephants, buffalos, lions, Kordofan Giraffes, pangolins and several primate, reptile and bird species. This overlap of fauna from two distinct biogeographical regions gives the area particular conservation interest.

**Criterion (ix):**Garamba National Park contains a mosaic of grasslands, wooded savannas, and patches of semi-deciduous forest that reflect a long-standing ecological transition between the Guineo-Congolian forest and the Sudano-Zambezian savanna zones. In the property, open savannas cover approximately 30% of the area and represent the only large expanses of open savanna in northern Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC). Their origin is most likely linked to historically high concentrations of large herbivores in the region. The park’s open savannas and woodlands form a dynamic system capable of shifting in either direction, primarily shaped by fire and herbivory, which operate independently within the park. Forest formations are relatively small but represent the climax vegetation of the region and contribute substantially to the ecosystem's richness.
Within the park, ecological processes such as natural fires, herbivore grazing, and seasonal flooding continue to shape the landscape. These processes drive shifts in vegetation composition and structure, maintaining a balance between open and wooded habitats. The property supports a healthy assemblage of large herbivores, including African Forest Elephants, Kordofan Giraffes, Common Hippopotamuses, African buffaloes. These large herbivores drive key ecological processes, which are in turn shaped by predator-prey dynamics involving significant populations of northern lions, spotted hyenas, and leopards. These processes illustrate an ecosystem that remains largely functional within its protected boundaries.
**Criterion (x):**Garamba National Park is part of a larger ecological system that once supported some of the highest concentrations of large mammals in Central Africa. Together with its buffer zone, the property hosts a wide variety of natural habitats, ranging from open savannas to dense forests, representing the full gradient of the forest-savanna transition. In addition, the property contains a vast aquatic ecosystem that includes large, sandy-bottomed rivers, waterways lined with gallery forests, and marshes supporting extensive stands of papyrus. These habitats provide critical areas for the in-situ conservation of globally threatened species and regional endemics.

Garamba National Park is home to over 150 mammal species, including 13 threatened species or subspecies, as well as seven species or subspecies that are endemic or sub-endemic to northeastern DRC and adjacent areas of South Sudan and northwestern Uganda. The property remains important for the conservation of a range of forest and savanna species including significant populations of African Forest Elephants, Kordofan Giraffes, Common Hippopotamuses, lions and four pangolins and several primate species. The avifauna comprises at least 459 species, including three regional endemic forms, 11 threatened species, and several species with highly restricted ranges. The reptile fauna includes 83 species, four of which are regional endemics and two of which are threatened. Amphibians account for 43 species, including three regional endemic forms.
**Integrity**
The boundaries of Garamba National Park correspond to those established at the time of its creation in 1938 and its inscription in 1980. They have clear legal recognition and provide a strong institutional basis for management. There are largely natural boundaries, formed by rivers (the Garamba, Dodo, Dungu, and Aka) which provide an unambiguous line of separation. The northern boundary is the international border with South Sudan, of which part also forms the southern boundary of Lantoto National Park. This clarity is logistically beneficial for survey work and for the park's management and anti-poaching patrols, as it leaves little room for disputing the park’s official extent.
The surrounding hunting domains (Gangala-na-Bodio, Mondo-Missa, and Azande) functioned since 1980 as a de facto buffer zone for the property, providing an additional layer of controlled land use and supporting ecological connectivity across the wider Garamba landscape. The renomination formally recognises the buffer zone to include portions of the three hunting domains extending up to 20 km from the property boundaries and covers an area of 544,943 ha. It encompasses some of the most intact areas of the surrounding landscape and contributes to maintaining ecological processes and habitat connectivity for wide-ranging species.

At the same time, the hunting domains have been affected by prolonged insecurity, weak governance, and pressures associated with armed incursions, transboundary transhumance, mining, and agricultural encroachment. Large-scale poaching, particularly associated with ivory and rhino horn trafficking, has caused severe declines in populations of key large mammals across the wider Garamba Complex, including the likely extinction of the Northern White Rhinoceros and significant declines in elephant populations.
**Protection and management requirements**
Garamba National Park benefits from a solid and multi-layered legal protection framework. Initially established by royal decree in 1938, its status has since been reinforced through national conservation laws most notably Law 14/003 of 2014 and through subsequent decrees regulating protected areas and the CorPSN (Corps pour la Protection des Parcs Nationaux). Garamba National Park is co-managed within a broader Garamba Complex, which includes three state-owned hunting domains (Gangala-na-Bodio, Mondo-Missa, and Azande) under a formal Public–Private Partnership (PPP) between the Institut Congolais pour la Conservation de la Nature (ICCN) and African Parks Network (APN). The arrangement establishes a shared management structure through the Garamba Management Foundation, which has a Board of Directors comprising four representatives from APN (including the Chair) and three from ICCN (including the Vice-Chair). This framework ensures transparent decision-making, balanced oversight, and alignment with national conservation legislation. It combines ICCN’s legal mandate with African Parks’ technical and operational expertise, providing a professional and performance-oriented management model. The park’s management organization is well-structured, comprising departments for biodiversity conservation, community development, law enforcement, tourism, and infrastructure, supported by a research and monitoring unit. These departments operate under the supervision of a management team comprised of a Chief of site or Park Director from APN, and a Deputy Chief of site from ICCN.

Garamba National Park operates under a Business Plan developed by APN and the ICCN, updated every five years to align with evolving conservation priorities. The Business Plan is guided by a 20-year vision outlined in a Long-Term Sustainability Strategy (2024-2044). The plan is actively used to guide daily operations alongside management objectives such as anti-poaching, habitat restoration, and community engagement. Key threats, such as armed poaching, illegal mining, and climate-driven habitat shifts, are addressed through targeted strategies like increased ranger patrols, drone surveillance, and community livelihood programs.

# Garamba National Park
###### Garamba National Park
The property, located in the north-eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo, forms part of one of the last extensive and continuous forest–savanna mosaic landscapes in Central Africa. Representing a major ecological transition zone between the Guineo-Congolian forest biome and the Sudanian savanna, it encompasses a diverse range of habitats, including grasslands, wooded savannas, semi-deciduous forests, rivers, gallery forests, marshes, and papyrus wetlands. Ecological processes such as fire, herbivory, and seasonal flooding continue to shape the landscape and maintain its forest–savanna dynamics. The park supports a rich assemblage of wildlife, including significant populations of African Forest Elephants, Kordofan Giraffes, Common Hippopotamuses, African buffaloes, lions, pangolins, and numerous primate species. It is home to more than 150 mammal species, 459 bird species, 83 reptile species, and 43 amphibian species, including threatened and regional endemic species.

###### Parc national de la Garamba
Le bien, situé dans le nord-est de la République démocratique du Congo, fait partie de l’une des dernières vastes mosaïques continues de forêts et de savanes d’Afrique centrale. Représentant une importante zone de transition écologique entre le biome forestier guinéo-congolais et la savane soudanienne, il englobe une grande diversité d’habitats, notamment des prairies, des savanes boisées, des forêts semi-décidues, des cours d’eau, des forêts-galeries, des marécages et des zones humides à papyrus. Des processus écologiques tels que les incendies naturels, l’herbivorie et les inondations saisonnières continuent de modeler le paysage et de maintenir la dynamique forêt-savane. Le parc abrite une faune d’une grande richesse, comprenant d’importantes populations d’éléphants de forêt d’Afrique, de girafes du Kordofan, d’hippopotames communs, de buffles d’Afrique, de lions, de pangolins, ainsi que de nombreuses espèces de primates. Il accueille plus de 150 espèces de mammifères, 459 espèces d’oiseaux, 83 espèces de reptiles et 43 espèces d’amphibiens, parmi lesquelles figurent des espèces menacées ainsi que des espèces endémiques à l’échelle régionale.

The World Heritage Committee,
1.   Having examined Documents WHC/26/48.COM/8B and WHC/26/48.COM/INF.8B2,  
2.   Approves the renomination of **Garamba National Park, Democratic Republic of the Congo**, on the World Heritage List on the basis of **criteria****(ix)** and **(x)**;  
3.   Adopts the following Statement of Outstanding Universal Value:
**Brief synthesis**
Garamba National Park is situated in the north-eastern region of the Democratic Republic of the Congo, within Haut-Uélé Province, adjacent to the international boundary with South Sudan. The property forms the ecological core of the larger Garamba Complex, which encompasses approximately 1,470,000 hectares and includes the Azande, Gangala-na-Bodio, and Mondo-Missa hunting domains. Together, these contiguous protected areas constitute one of the last extensive and continuous forest–savanna mosaic landscapes in Central Africa, representing a critical ecological transition zone between the Guineo-Congolian forest biome and the Sudanian savanna. The property covers an area of 512,736 hectares. It is surrounded by a formally designated buffer zone comprising portions of the three adjacent hunting domains, extending up to 20 km from the park boundaries and covering an additional 544,943 hectares. The property is important for the conservation of a range of forest and savanna species, including forest elephants, buffalos, lions, Kordofan Giraffes, pangolins and several primate, reptile and bird species. This overlap of fauna from two distinct biogeographical regions gives the area particular conservation interest.

**Criterion (ix):**Garamba National Park contains a mosaic of grasslands, wooded savannas, and patches of semi-deciduous forest that reflect a long-standing ecological transition between the Guineo-Congolian forest and the Sudano-Zambezian savanna zones. In the property, open savannas cover approximately 30% of the area and represent the only large expanses of open savanna in northern Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC). Their origin is most likely linked to historically high concentrations of large herbivores in the region. The park’s open savannas and woodlands form a dynamic system capable of shifting in either direction, primarily shaped by fire and herbivory, which operate independently within the park. Forest formations are relatively small but represent the climax vegetation of the region and contribute substantially to the ecosystem's richness.
Within the park, ecological processes such as natural fires, herbivore grazing, and seasonal flooding continue to shape the landscape. These processes drive shifts in vegetation composition and structure, maintaining a balance between open and wooded habitats. The property supports a healthy assemblage of large herbivores, including African Forest Elephants, Kordofan Giraffes, Common Hippopotamuses, African buffaloes. These large herbivores drive key ecological processes, which are in turn shaped by predator-prey dynamics involving significant populations of northern lions, spotted hyenas, and leopards. These processes illustrate an ecosystem that remains largely functional within its protected boundaries.
**Criterion (x):**Garamba National Park is part of a larger ecological system that once supported some of the highest concentrations of large mammals in Central Africa. Together with its buffer zone, the property hosts a wide variety of natural habitats, ranging from open savannas to dense forests, representing the full gradient of the forest-savanna transition. In addition, the property contains a vast aquatic ecosystem that includes large, sandy-bottomed rivers, waterways lined with gallery forests, and marshes supporting extensive stands of papyrus. These habitats provide critical areas for the in-situ conservation of globally threatened species and regional endemics.

Garamba National Park is home to over 150 mammal species, including 13 threatened species or subspecies, as well as seven species or subspecies that are endemic or sub-endemic to northeastern DRC and adjacent areas of South Sudan and northwestern Uganda. The property remains important for the conservation of a range of forest and savanna species including significant populations of African Forest Elephants, Kordofan Giraffes, Common Hippopotamuses, lions and four pangolins and several primate species. The avifauna comprises at least 459 species, including three regional endemic forms, 11 threatened species, and several species with highly restricted ranges. The reptile fauna includes 83 species, four of which are regional endemics and two of which are threatened. Amphibians account for 43 species, including three regional endemic forms.
**Integrity**
The boundaries of Garamba National Park correspond to those established at the time of its creation in 1938 and its inscription in 1980. They have clear legal recognition and provide a strong institutional basis for management. There are largely natural boundaries, formed by rivers (the Garamba, Dodo, Dungu, and Aka) which provide an unambiguous line of separation. The northern boundary is the international border with South Sudan, of which part also forms the southern boundary of Lantoto National Park. This clarity is logistically beneficial for survey work and for the park's management and anti-poaching patrols, as it leaves little room for disputing the park’s official extent.
The surrounding hunting domains (Gangala-na-Bodio, Mondo-Missa, and Azande) functioned since 1980 as a de facto buffer zone for the property, providing an additional layer of controlled land use and supporting ecological connectivity across the wider Garamba landscape. The renomination formally recognises the buffer zone to include portions of the three hunting domains extending up to 20 km from the property boundaries and covers an area of 544,943 ha. It encompasses some of the most intact areas of the surrounding landscape and contributes to maintaining ecological processes and habitat connectivity for wide-ranging species.

At the same time, the hunting domains have been affected by prolonged insecurity, weak governance, and pressures associated with armed incursions, transboundary transhumance, mining, and agricultural encroachment. Large-scale poaching, particularly associated with ivory and rhino horn trafficking, has caused severe declines in populations of key large mammals across the wider Garamba Complex, including the likely extinction of the Northern White Rhinoceros and significant declines in elephant populations.
**Protection and management requirements**
Garamba National Park benefits from a solid and multi-layered legal protection framework. Initially established by royal decree in 1938, its status has since been reinforced through national conservation laws most notably Law 14/003 of 2014 and through subsequent decrees regulating protected areas and the CorPSN (Corps pour la Protection des Parcs Nationaux). Garamba National Park is co-managed within a broader Garamba Complex, which includes three state-owned hunting domains (Gangala-na-Bodio, Mondo-Missa, and Azande) under a formal Public–Private Partnership (PPP) between the Institut Congolais pour la Conservation de la Nature (ICCN) and African Parks Network (APN). The arrangement establishes a shared management structure through the Garamba Management Foundation, which has a Board of Directors comprising four representatives from APN (including the Chair) and three from ICCN (including the Vice-Chair). This framework ensures transparent decision-making, balanced oversight, and alignment with national conservation legislation. It combines ICCN’s legal mandate with African Parks’ technical and operational expertise, providing a professional and performance-oriented management model. The park’s management organization is well-structured, comprising departments for biodiversity conservation, community development, law enforcement, tourism, and infrastructure, supported by a research and monitoring unit. These departments operate under the supervision of a management team comprised of a Chief of site or Park Director from APN, and a Deputy Chief of site from ICCN.

Garamba National Park operates under a Business Plan developed by APN and the ICCN, updated every five years to align with evolving conservation priorities. The Business Plan is guided by a 20-year vision outlined in a Long-Term Sustainability Strategy (2024-2044). The plan is actively used to guide daily operations alongside management objectives such as anti-poaching, habitat restoration, and community engagement. Key threats, such as armed poaching, illegal mining, and climate-driven habitat shifts, are addressed through targeted strategies like increased ranger patrols, drone surveillance, and community livelihood programs.

# Garamba National Park
## Full assessment
### Assessment information
For more than a decade, the park and its surrounding buffer zones were used as a cover by the Lord’s Resistance Army (LRA) (a rebel group originating in Uganda). This armed militia wreaked havoc amongst local communities and destroyed the park headquarters at Nagero in January 2009 (with the loss of 10 lives), but subsequently became increasingly fragmented and dispersed (Titeca and Costeur, 2015). By the time of the last UNESCO/IUCN Reactive Monitoring mission in 2016, they had mostly moved away from areas previously occupied in the park and Azande Hunting Area into the south-eastern areas of CAR (UNESCO and IUCN, 2016). For some time, personnel of the government’s Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of Congo (FARDC), who were tasked with driving out remaining elements of LRA and improving security, were also contributing to the escalation of poaching (Titeca, 2013). Measures have subsequently been taken to ensure that the FARDC are no longer a threat to the park (UNESCO and IUCN, 2016; UNESCO, 2017). As a result of increased actions, the LRA have now been chased off the property; however, minor issues with local poachers, South Sudanese poachers, Mbororo, and other armed groups persist (IUCN Consultation, 2020). Recent reports note that armed conflicts have been caused by a mixture of groups, including the LRA, but also South Sudanese rebels, local poachers, FARDC, Mbororo, etc. (Titeca and Edmond, 2019). In 2020, anti-poaching collaborations between ICCN, African Parks, FARDC, and local authorities were further strengthened, and FARDC forces supported surveillance efforts in and around the site (State Party of the DRC, 2020). As a result of a combination of strong efforts by African Parks and relative calm in South Sudan, Garamba is currently experiencing low levels of insecurity, although it is likely that the stability may only be temporary and therefore insecurity remains a potential future threat (IUCN Consultation, 2020).

# Garamba National Park
## Full assessment
### Assessment information
Garamba National Park has faced severe threats from illegal hunting, particularly targeting elephants and historically the critically endangered northern white rhinoceros, which was declared functionally extinct in the wild in 2008 (UNESCO, 2023). Illegal commercial hunting over the past 45 years has resulted in significant declines of all wildlife populations on the site (ICCN, 2010; UNESCO and IUCN, 2016; Titeca et al., 2020). In 2012, poachers killed 22 elephants in a single incident, and between 2012 and 2015, the park lost nearly 90% of its elephant population due to ivory poaching (African Parks, 2023). The park was inscribed on the List of World Heritage in Danger multiple times, most recently in 1996, due to poaching crises exacerbated by armed groups and cross-border militias operating in the region (UNESCO, 2023). Ivory poaching, driven by international demand, has drastically reduced elephant populations, with Garamba’s elephants noted for their genetic distinctiveness (UNESCO, 2023). Additionally, the park’s proximity to conflict zones in Central Africa has allowed organized poaching networks, such as the Lord’s Resistance Army (LRA) and Sudanese poachers from the SPLA, to exploit instability, using advanced weaponry and even helicopters (African Parks, 2023). This illegal hunting undermines biodiversity, disrupts ecosystems, and threatens the park’s Outstanding Universal Value, while also endangering local communities and rangers. For instance, in 2016, a ranger was killed during an anti-poaching operation, highlighting the risks faced by conservation staff (IUCN, 2020).

# Garamba National Park
## Full assessment
### Assessment information
Animal populations remain significantly reduced compared to their initial state at the time of the site's inscription. However, it is essential to note that population estimates for elephants (latest estimate in 2023) and Kordofan giraffes (latest estimate in 2024) show very encouraging results, with annual growth rates exceeding 10% for both species. A new aerial survey, planned for 2025 and covering more species, is expected to confirm the upward trend already observed during the last survey conducted in 2021. A very positive sign is that poaching trends for key species, particularly elephants and giraffes, have significantly declined since 2017 (State Party of DRC, 2024). Over the past five years, only 4 elephant carcasses with evidence of poaching have been detected in the complex, compared to 91 in 2016 and 50 in 2017, for example. The quantity of bushmeat seized annually does not show an increasing trend (454 kg, 139 kg, 234 kg, and 100 kg in 2020, 2021, 2022, 2023, and 2024, respectively). No poached giraffe carcasses have been found since 2017 (State Party of DRC, 2024).

# Garamba National Park
## Full assessment
### Assessment information
Efforts to combat illegal hunting include strengthened anti-poaching patrols, aerial surveillance, and partnerships with organizations like African Parks Network, which has co-managed Garamba since 2005 (African Parks, 2023). For example, African Parks has deployed a specialized canine unit and drones to track poachers, leading to a significant reduction in elephant poaching incidents in recent years (African Parks, 2023). However, challenges persist due to the park’s vast size, limited resources, and ongoing insecurity from armed groups, including the LRA and other militias, which continue to operate in the region (UNESCO, 2023). Despite some progress, Poaching remains a critical threat. For instance, in 2020, a joint operation between Garamba rangers and Congolese military forces resulted in the arrest of several poachers and the confiscation of illegal firearms, underscoring the need for continued collaboration (African Parks, 2023). In 2024, foot patrols covered 58% and air patrols 98% of the property (State Party of DRC, 2024). Anti-poaching efforts must be proactively continued to ensure both the full eradication of poaching in the site and the recovery of key species.

## Democratic Republic of The Congo
_Immense savannahs, grasslands and woodlands, threaded with gallery forests and swampy depressions, protect a wide range of animals, especially the four large mammals, elephant, giraffe, hippopotamus and the critically endangered northern white rhinoceros. This is much larger than the black rhino, and less than thirty individuals remain in the wild. It is one of the world’s twelve most threatened large animals._
_Threats to the Site: The Park was placed on the List of the World Heritage in Danger between 1984 and 1992 because of a serious decline in the rhinoceros population. After measures taken by the World Heritage Committee, IUCN, WWF, the Frankfort Zoological Society and the national authorities, the population recovered from 15 to around 35 animals. Since 1996 civil disorder in the east of the country has led to widespread attacks on the Park. Equipment was looted, outposts destroyed and several staff deserted. The site was returned to the_[_in Danger_](file:///D:/toc/mainf4.htm)_list. Poachers from the Sudan and Uganda are still very destructive but the remaining staff retain control of the southern third of the Park. Threats to the animal populations will not cease until adequate funding permits the enforcement of law and order._

## Country
* * *
Democratic Republic of the Congo

## Name
* * *
Garamba National Park

## Natural World Heritage Site In Danger
* * *
1980: Inscribed on the World Heritage List under Natural Criteria vii and x.
1984-92 & 1996 +: Listed as a World Heritage site in Danger due to decline in the rhinoceros population.

## Statement of Outstanding Universal Value [pending]
* * *

## IUCN Management Category
* * *
II National Park

## Biogeographical Province
* * *
East African Woodland / Savanna (3.05.04)

## Geographical Location
* * *
In the far northeast of the Democratic Republic of the Congo on the border with Sudan: 3°45'-4°41'N, 28°48'-30°00'E.

## Dates and History of Establishment
* * *
1938: Instituted by decree as Garamba National Park to protect giraffe and northern white rhinoceros;
1969: The National Institute for Nature Conservation received responsibility for it by Decree 69/72;
1975: The _Institut Zaïrois pour la Conservation de la Nature_ (IZCN) made responsible for the park under the State Commission for the Environment, Nature Conservation and Tourism;
1984-92 &1996: Listed as endangered because of increased poaching, and threats to the endangered white rhinoceros and of infrastructure, resulting from the civil war in Sudan.

## Land Tenure
* * *
Government, in Uele district of Orientale province. Administered by the _Institut Congolais_ (formerly _Zairois_) _pour la Conservation de la Nature_ (IZCN / ICCN).

## Area
* * *
492,000 ha. (500,000 ha, UNESCO,2008). Surrounded by three hunting areas totalling about 1,000,000 ha: Reserve Azande to the west, Reserve Mondo-Missa to the east and Reserve Gangala na Bodio to the south. Contiguous on the northeast with the proposed Lantoto National Park in Sudan.

## Altitude
* * *
710m to 1,061m

## Physical Features
* * *
The Park covers a vast undulating plateau parkland, principally long-grass and dense bush savanna, shaped by fire. It slopes southwest from the watershed between the Nile and Congo rivers, part of an ancient peneplain interrupted by mostly granitic inselbergs, threaded by gallery forests, with large marshland depressions. The main rivers are the Dungu on the southern boundary, the Aka along the western boundary and the Garamba within the Park (IZCN, 1980).

## Climate
* * *
The tropical climate has a semi-moist rainy season from March to November with a mean annual rainfall averaging about 1260mm. Average annual temperatures are between 20° and 30° C, with a dry period from November to March, when temperatures range from 6°C to 39°C and hot dry north-easterly winds are common (Hillman-Smith, 1989).

## Vegetation
* * *
The Park's position, between the Guinean and Sudanese biogeographic realms, makes it unusually diverse. In fact it is within a WWF/IUCN Centre of Plant Diversity. It covers three biomes: gallery forest with forest clumps and marshland; aquatic and semi-aquatic associations; and savannas ranging from dense savanna woodland to nearly treeless grassland. The densely wooded savanna, relict gallery forests, and the papyrus marshes of the north and west give way in the centre to more open tree-bush savanna, which merges into the long grass savanna that covers most of the Park.
The savanna woodlands are often dominated by _Combretum_ spp. and _Terminalia mollis_. Accompanying dominant species include _Hymenocardia acida_, _Bauhinia thonningii_, _Dombeya quinqueseta_, _Acacia_, _Grewia_ and _Bridelia_ spp., _Albizzia glaberrima_ and _Erythrina abyssinica_. Gallery forests and forest patches contain _Erythrophleum suaveolens_, _Chlorophora excelsa_, _Irvingia smithii_, _Klainedoxa_ sp.,_Spathodea campanulata_, _Ficus_ spp. and African mahaoganies _Khaya anthotheca_ (VU) and _K. grandifolia_ (VU). Sudanian woodland grows towards the north-eastern part of the park, which is dominated by _Isoberlinia doka_ with scattered _Uapaca somon_. Marshlands are dominated by _Cyperus papyrus_ and _Mitragyna rubrostipulacea_ (Hillman-Smith, 1989).
The main species of the long-grass savanna are _Loudetia arundinacea_ and various _Hyparrhenia_ species, which in September can grow over 2m high, with the tallest grass _Urelytrum giganteum_ up to 5m. There are occasional scattered _Kigelia africana_ and _Vitex doniana_ trees. It is dissected by numerous small rivers with valley grasslands and papyrus swamps.

## Vegetation
According to Davis _et al._ (1994), there are approximately 1,000 vascular plant species, of which some 5% are endemic. Useful plants found growing in the Park include _Erythrophleum guineense_, _Nauclea latifolia_, _Terminalia mollis_ (building material), _Vitex doniana_ (medicinal); _Spathodea campanulata_ (ornamental); _Cyperus papyrus_, _Thalia welwitschii_ (ropes, mats, baskets); _Hymenocardia acida_, _Hyparrhenia diplandra_, _Loudetia phragmitoides_, _L.simplex_, _Pennisetum simplex_ (fuel), _P. purpureum, Hallea stipulosa_, _Imperata cylindrica_, _Khaya anthotheca_ and _Leersia hexandra_ (Davis _et al_., 1994).

**The Kordofan giraffe in the Democratic Republic of Congo is found only in Garamba National Park** – a UNESCO World Heritage Site that has long been on the UNESCO “List in Danger” because of poaching, armed conflict and habitat loss (though the park has recently been removed from that list). Below is a practical guide to spotting these critically‑endangered giants on your June 2025 visit. | Topic | Key details | |-------|-------------| | **Where** | **Garamba National Park** – Haut‑Uélé Province, north‑eastern DRC, bordering South Sudan. The park covers ~492 000 ha and is part of the larger Garamba‑Complex (park + buffer zones). | | **Why it matters** | The park is the **only remaining wild population of the Kordofan giraffe (Giraffa camelopardalis antiquorum)** in the entire country, with an estimated 75–100 individuals (2024 data).¹ | | **Best time to see them** | **Dry season (December – March)** gives the best wildlife visibility and easier travel conditions, but Kordofan giraffes have been observed throughout the year, including the wet season (April – October). If you travel in June, be prepared for rains but you can still see giraffes, especially in the park’s open savannah sections. | | **Getting there** | 1. **Flight to Kisangani** (international hub) or **Entebbe, Uganda** → **Kisangani** (private charter). 2. **Charter to Nagero airstrip** inside Garamba (managed by African Parks).
3. **Ground transport**: Park officials provide vehicle accompaniment from the airstrip to the great savannah zones. | | **Permits & bookings** | • **Entrance permit** – issued by the **Inde Institut Congolais pour la Conservation de la Nature (ICCN)** in partnership with **African Parks**.
• **Safari booking** – must be made **at least 2 months in advance** through African Parks or a certified tour operator.
• **Visitor centre**: Nagero (park headquarters); day‑tours usually run 9 am – 4 pm. | | **Safety & security** | • The park’s security situation is **more stable than in the past** thanks to a joint anti‑poaching effort between ICCN, African Parks, FARDC and local communities.
• Still a **high‑risk area** for travelers; follow all instructions from park rangers and never venture beyond authorized routes.
• It is advisable to travel with a **local guide** familiar with the terrain and current security conditions. | | **What to expect** | • Giraffe can be seen **spotted in the savannahs and along the Garamba and Dungu rivers**; they are most active during early morning and late afternoon.
• Other megafauna: African forest elephant, common hippopotamus, African buffalo, lion, and numerous bird species. | --- ## Practical itinerary for June 2025 | Day | Activity | |-----|----------| | **Day 1** | Arrive in **Kisangani**, transfer to a charter flight to **Nagero** (in‑park airstrip). | | **Day 2** | **Orientation briefing** with the African Parks ranger team. 10‑hour game drive covering the high‑savannah (great giraffe habitat). | | **Day 3** | **Giraffe‑specialised circuit** (carried out in the **"Giraffe Corridor"** identified by recent aerial surveys).
